analysis.one_liner: Lets people sue government officials who violate their rights by eliminating qualified immunity.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would let people sue officials who violate their constitutional rights even when the right was not clearly established, has sat in the House Judiciary Committee without a hearing since its introduction.
analysis.plain_summary: When a police officer or other government official violates someone's constitutional rights, a Supreme Court-made doctrine called qualified immunity usually blocks the victim from winning damages unless they can point to a prior court case with nearly identical facts. This bill would amend the federal civil rights statute (42 U.S.C. 1983) to make clear that neither good faith nor a lack of clearly established law is a defense. The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and has had no action since.
analysis.who_benefits: People whose constitutional rights are violated by state and local officials acting under color of law — most often in police misconduct cases — would be able to recover money damages even when the violation was in a gray area of the law, making it easier to hold officials accountable and creating a stronger deterrent.

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds a subsection to 42 U.S.C. 1983 stating that it is not a defense that the defendant acted in good faith, believed the conduct was lawful, or that the right was not clearly established at the time [S2].
The bill's findings recount that qualified immunity is a judge-made doctrine dating to the late 1960s and 1982, and that the 1871 civil rights statute Congress wrote contained no such immunity [S2].
Under current doctrine, victims can lose lawsuits solely because no prior case had almost identical facts, which has severely limited recovery under section 1983 [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Government officials who violate rights would face personal legal exposure, and state and local governments (which typically indemnify their employees and pay judgments) would bear higher litigation and payout costs; courts would also see more cases going to trial rather than being dismissed early.
analysis.who_pays_short: Officials, police departments, and local governments

drawbacks.text: Officers and other officials could face personal liability even when they made a reasonable, good-faith effort to follow the law, a cost that could be passed on through higher insurance and settlement costs for local governments [S2].

Supporters of qualified immunity argue the doctrine protects officials from second-guessing of split-second decisions; this bill would eliminate that protection entirely rather than reforming it [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people harmed by constitutional violations, the change is substantial: the 'clearly established' requirement is the single biggest barrier to recovering damages, and removing it would let many valid claims proceed that courts now dismiss. The costs fall mainly on governments and officials, which is the point — but the bill does not address concerns that officers could face liability for honest mistakes, and taxpayers may ultimately fund the judgments their governments indemnify.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and has had no hearing, markup, or vote since, so it cannot reach the floor under current committee control.

narrative.text: Rep. Ayanna Pressley introduced the Ending Qualified Immunity Act on May 23, 2025, with 18 Democratic cosponsors [S1][S3].
The House referred the bill to the Judiciary Committee the same day; the action history shows no further action of any kind [S4].
No hearing or markup has been scheduled, and no version of the bill has been introduced in the Senate [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill has gone nowhere, government officials and law enforcement keep the qualified immunity defense that shields them from damages in civil rights lawsuits, while people whose rights are violated remain unable to recover in the many cases the doctrine screens out.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Officials and police keep immunity shield

for.name: Rep. Ayanna Pressley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Ending Qualified Immunity Act and assembled 18 original cosponsors.

for.name: 18 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, including Reps. Jayapal, Ocasio-Cortez, Tlaib, Schakowsky, and others.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Chair of the committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; the record shows no committee action after the May 23, 2025 referral.

against.name: House Republican majority
against.role: Majority controlling the House floor and committee calendars
against.what_they_did: Controls the committee schedule and floor agenda; qualified immunity legislation has not been brought forward this Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 18 cosponsors and the sponsor are Democrats; no Republican support appears in the record, and the Republican-led Judiciary Committee has taken no action [S3][S4].

industries.note: Ending qualified immunity would expose officers to personal damages liability for constitutional violations, the outcome unions have consistently opposed. The bill would deter misconduct that falls on ordinary people, but police organizations view it as stripping protection for good-faith mistakes.

Municipalities typically pay judgments on behalf of employees, so removing qualified immunity would raise litigation, settlement, and insurance costs for cities and counties — costs ultimately borne by taxpayers.

analysis.trajectory: With a Republican-led House Judiciary Committee that has taken no action in months and no Senate companion, the bill is on the standard path for majority-opposition legislation: it will very likely sit without a hearing until the 119th Congress ends in January 2027, dying without a vote.
